speaker: James Frith
subheading: Societal Impact of AI: Government Policy
text:
The Government’s principle is to regulate at the time of deployment or at use. I understand the right hon. Gentleman’s argument, but it is important that we strike the right balance between innovation and regulation. Of course, as I will come on to discuss in more detail, where there have been examples of harm we must call that out and call in those who caused them.

The Government have already committed to ambitious plans to transform services. For a radiologist, that means access to the best tools for detecting cancer—tools that can save lives and cut waiting lists in our NHS. The public sector is where it is perhaps most crucial that the Government ensure that we embed frameworks, standards and guidance to ensure that AI is deployed in a way that is fair, transparent and accountable. We are doing so with the data and AI ethics framework, the AI playbook, and transparency standards that ensure the public can understand how systems are used.

We are also supporting UK firms that provide third-party AI-assurance ecosystems, demonstrating that AI systems are safe and reliable as well as creating new jobs. That is critical not just for risk management but for building businesses, building confidence in those deploying AI, and building trust in the systems we use. To the points that were made about the job market, AI has the potential to enhance job roles and the performance of each of us at work, but it is necessary and reasonable, as my hon. Friend the Member for Poole pointed out, to distinguish the jobs that are most at risk—those least likely to be enhanced and most likely to be replaced. That is a very reasonable proposition. We recognise that one of the primary areas where people will interact with AI is in the labour market.

To zone in on labour markets, and the issue of young people and entry-level jobs, an estimated 12.8% of all people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training. That goes well beyond data-entry or access-level jobs, or a potential shift of culture in relation to entry-level jobs. To date, there is little conclusive evidence that AI is reducing employment. However, the International Monetary Fund estimates that around 70% of UK workers are in exposed occupations. Around half of those exposed workers are in high complementary roles, where AI will enhance rather than replace their work.

The Government are committed to supporting the worker experience through the AI transition, and have a proud record of advancing workers’ rights. To that end, earlier this year the Government established the AI and the future of work unit, bringing together expertise from across Departments and industry to monitor how AI is affecting jobs, wages and opportunity in real time. We are putting in place the institutions, data and cross-Government co-ordination needed to ensure that AI transforms the labour market, that workers are supported and that opportunities are widely shared across society.

We are also investing in people, because the opportunities of AI will be realised only if the workforce are equipped to harness them. That is why we have launched one of the most ambitious skills programmes anywhere in the world. Our AI skills boost programme is already delivering results. In an answer given to the House last week, I referred to the early careers funding and work on curriculum reforms to come, such as an AI-inclusive GCSE in computing.

This is about ensuring that workers at every stage of their career, and whether in small businesses, large firms or public services, have the tools that they need to thrive in an AI-enabled economy. AI will have—is having—seismic impacts on our working lives and productivity, and we must embrace the democracy this gives us. We must democratise access to AI to ensure that communities across the country reap the benefits. Central to that effort is ensuring that support is delivered to the graduates and young people entering the world of work for the first time. Much has been made of the rising level of NEETs. Programmes such as TechLocal are creating new jobs, traineeships and professional training, while scholarships and fellowships are supporting the next generation of researchers and innovators.

Nobody is waiting 25 years to tackle the threats, however. AI harms are very real, and we do not sit idly by when it comes to tackling them. We are not standing still. The AI Security Institute is conducting world-leading research to understand the capabilities and impacts of advanced AI. In response to the generation of vile and degrading non-consensual sexual deepfakes on Grok earlier this year, the Prime Minister himself, and the Government, stood up to Grok and X and won that fight. We have criminalised the creation of non-consensual sexual deepfakes and legislated to require platforms to remove them. Separately, we have banned nudification apps and criminalised AI tools designed to create sexual abuse material, as well as learning the importance of sovereignty when considering the recent switching off of the latest Anthropic AI tool.

I was asked a specific question about the social media ban. I was a proud early adopter of the policy and I am pleased to say that it remains the Government’s intention to update the House before recess.

The UK is proactively responding to the AI revolution—we are shaping it. AI has extraordinary potential to improve healthcare, accelerate scientific discovery, personalise education, strengthen public services and drive economic growth. We will harness the opportunities across every region and community to shape UK society for the better for all.

speaker: Baroness Ramsey of Wall Heath
heading: Business Hiring - Question
text: I thank the noble Lord for his question but remind him that, thanks to our industrial strategy, employment is rising. Employment rights are improving too. We are determined to reduce unemployment further, especially among the young, which is why we are investing so much in the youth guarantee and are poised to go further when the Milburn review reports back later this year. I am aware of the situation where AI recruiting is impacting on graduate appointments and recruitment, and I am also aware that the Government have issued guidance to employers to ensure that this is a reducing problem, not an increasing one.

speaker: Baroness Lloyd of Effra
heading: EU Technological Sovereignty Package - Question
text: Investments that are backed by, for example, the sovereign AI fund must of course abide by UK laws, including copyright laws. However, this also goes to the point about AI technology in terms of discerning values and the understanding of everybody, from children to workers to older populations, about how to safely adopt AI. The assurance market in AI is something that we are backing very strongly, so that people have real clarity about the underlying credentials of the AI that they use.

speaker: Ben Small
heading: BILLS
subheading: Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Yet again, we find ourselves in this place debating a bill that's got a title that's pretty hard to disagree with. Labor want to pretend that this bill, the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill 2026, is about funding and student places. They want to pretend that it's about increasing university funding to help poor kids, Indigenous kids and kids from the bush—kids from regional electorates—to get a go. If that's all this bill did, then the coalition would be in full support of it.

However, we have to reserve our position at this stage because this bill needs to go through a Senate inquiry so Australians can have their say. The reality is that, time and time again, through these inquiries, we see the sort of feedback that points out glaring holes in the government's legislation. We saw that just in the winter break, with the Senate gambling inquiry, which was fought tooth and nail by the government but exposed clear holes in the bill. And so it is with the Universities Accord (Opening the Doors of Opportunity) Bill that we're here to debate today.

Once we've received that evidence and the Australian people have had their say, we will consider what our position ultimately is in the Senate and what amendments are necessary, because this bill is worthy of close scrutiny. It makes significant structural changes to the higher education system. We note concerns that have already emerged from the tertiary education sector about the consultation process the government has run, and that includes the fact that universities hadn't seen this bill before it was tabled in the parliament, that there are elements of the bill's drafting that surprise the tertiary education sector, that no exposure draft has been released and that stakeholders have been shown limited material under strict confidentiality arrangements. If the government had nothing to hide and this bill did all that it is purported to do and nothing else, one wonders why such poor consultation was conducted under such secrecy.

If the bill ultimately comes to a vote in the House before that Senate committee reports, we will find ourselves in uncertain territory. But it is appropriate that, as a party of alternative government, we take the time, we consult and we get our position right.

Let's consider what the problems are with our universities today. Unfortunately, they either have lost or are losing their social licence in Australia, and I believe it's because, for too many years now, universities in Australia have pursued indoctrination over education time and time again. What should be institutions that are homes of freedom of speech and freedom of academic integrity are, in fact, places of censorship, academic pile-ons and ideological confrontation.

Universities Australia held a summit this year, and the whole sector focused on their social licence. They did so because it's reflected in the data that domestic enrolments in universities are falling. In 2022, there were some 1.1 million domestic students studying at university in Australia. According to the most recent data, that number has fallen since the Albanese government came to office. It is now the lowest number of enrolments since 2019, and it is getting lower. That sends a very stark message from both the boots and the wallets of Australian students: their confidence in the Australian tertiary sector is declining.

According to the Department of Education, since 2022, when the Albanese government came to power, the ratio of students to teaching staff has increased, and the number of administrative, technical and operational staff is growing twice as fast as that of frontline teaching and research staff. That's on the department's own numbers.

The 2025 Quality Indicators for Learning and Teaching Graduate Outcomes Survey recorded a record-low graduate satisfaction of 74.9 per cent. I'll say that again. This year's survey recorded record-low graduate satisfaction among young Australians who are taking the time and incurring the cost of pursuing a degree at an Australian university. That's an appalling outcome. Undergraduate ratings for student support and services were even lower—71.2 per cent in 2023 and 2024, the lowest since 2015. Polling from the universities themselves reveals that the proportion of Australians with either 'quite a lot' or 'a great deal' of confidence in Australian universities has fallen. This reflects that loss of licence to operate in Australia that we see from institutions that pursue indoctrination over education.

Additionally, we've seen the government rip the guts out of research in this country—the same research that should drive productivity in our economy. It is one of the many reasons that productivity is absolutely flatlining in Australia, and we see a real loss of incomes as real GDP per capita sees the largest fall in living standards in the developed world. This has included cutting more than $2.3 billion out of university research through cuts to the Australia's Economic Accelerator program and abolishing the Trailblazer Universities Program, which saw co-investment by government and industry into research totalling more than $1.02 billion. We've seen the government slash our research capacity program by more than $920 million since the coalition was last in office. It is a cut which is significantly magnified in its effects because of the runaway inflation that we see in the economy today. On the government's own numbers, research spending in this country is projected to reach a decade low in 2029.

We haven't been the only ones to notice. Complaints by students and staff to TEQSA, the regulator, have almost quadrupled, from 237 complaints in 2022 to 942 last year. There is a serious problem in our university sector, and this bill, unfortunately, addresses none of those concerns. Safety data is particularly bad when you dive into the detail of those TEQSA complaints, because, in 2022, there were 16 TEQSA complaints in relation to gender based violence and other wellbeing and safety. It is now 76. Those figures don't include new data from the National Student Ombudsman, which received 1,711 complaints in its first six months.

Juxtaposed against that appalling deterioration in the safety of university campuses we've seen a spectacle, week after week, of encampments preaching hate against our country, against democracy and particularly against Jewish Australians. It is a shameful spectacle that sees ordinary Australian students, who have every right to get to the classes they're paying for, denied easy access and freedom of movement on their own university campuses by these extremists.

That has led to extraordinary levels of racist abuse and hatred on university campuses, as measured by the Racism@Uni survey. Above all, Jewish Australian students came out at the pointy end of that abuse and that hatred. But we believe that ultimately it stems from the basic failure of university leadership across the country to respond properly to the antisemitic hatred that we saw explode in Australia in October 2023. When you don't step in to stop encampments on campuses targeting one group of Australians, you send a message that it's actually okey. That's how university leadership has failed young Australians and indeed our country. With more than half of Australia's universities dropping in the world rankings in June this year, it comes as little wonder to us on the coalition side.

The universities themselves are complaining about having to comply with more than 300 pieces of legislation and regulation—which, admittedly, would have occurred under the watch of previous governments as well. But, based on a submission by TEQSA itself, there are now 15 different regulators and oversight bodies that universities report to. You might think that the 'opening the doors of opportunity' bill would be doing Australian universities a service by slashing the red tape and regulation that the university sector confronts. But, alas, we move on.

We've got repeated scandals in Australia about overseas cheating factories being used as a way to a degree. That diminishes the value of the Australian degrees that young people are paying good money for in this country. And over it all, of course, we've got the sector-wide challenge of confronting AI and the challenges it poses in a university setting. If AI is being used to mark work done by students, it makes humans redundant and the degree they receive pretty worthless. It's a massive challenge, and it's not being adequately addressed by the sector or by this bill.

So the message is pretty simple. Under Labor, our universities have become demonstrably, measurably worse as they have pursued a policy of indoctrination, not education. This bill, in centralising significant power over universities and higher education providers in the hands of the minister, is a central concern. It is absolutely beyond doubt that the minister has the best baritone in the building, but that doesn't make him the savant of all things when it comes to education and tertiary education. So we need to consider this very carefully as a bill that moves towards a centrally managed higher education system in our country, because the minister and indeed future ministers would gain extensive powers over domestic Commonwealth supported places, international student allocations, demand-driven higher education course places, the conditions placed on tertiary providers, needs based funding, and the priorities and directions given to ATEC.

That's a pretty startling sort of remit to give to one minister of any political stripe, because while these powers could be used for good—to address future serious policy problems within the sector—they also raise significant concern about competition, institutional autonomy, efficiency, parliamentary oversight and the degree of latitude afforded by ministerial discretion.

We do concede, though, in light of the foregoing, that the university sector itself faces some real problems. We've got quality concerns leading to that deterioration in the rankings of Australian universities. We've got the undeniable challenge and opportunity that AI presents to the university sector. We've seen that terrible rise in the scourge of antisemitism and the social cohesion challenges it presents, not only on our university campuses but, indeed, across society more broadly. We've got the situation with international student pressures in the context of managing Australia's migration system, which undeniably has seen the numbers too high and the standards too low overall. On the coalition side, we're honest about what we will do when it comes to tackling migration and getting the numbers down. We need the government to do the same. I look forward to Minister Burke finally making it to the Press Club to give that speech, which he was gagged from only last week.

We see a bill before the House that gives a future government powerful tools to respond to those problems, but there are legitimate concerns. Again, that's where our call for a Senate inquiry into this legislation is so important. It is important because these powers could be used by a minister in the national interest if they were applied carefully and transparently. There may well be a compelling case for additional safeguards to ensure that a future minister would make decisions that would benefit not only the university sector but every Australian student who forks out for a degree and, indeed, our nation overall. They could tackle some of the issues we saw, like our flatlining productivity, by enlivening research in Australia once more and seeing greater cooperation between the commercial and tertiary sectors—perhaps supercharged with the effective adoption of AI across the sector. We could see those very significant social cohesion concerns challenged and then corrected over time, if this legislation gets that balance right. It could see the freedom of speech and academic integrity restored to our university campuses, as it ought to be, and leave the nation a more prosperous place.

speaker: Raff Ciccone
heading: ADJOURNMENT
subheading: Australian Defence Force Parliamentary Program, Australian Strategic Policy Institute
text:
I rise this evening to welcome Flight Lieutenant Evans to Parliament House this week. He is spending his time with me and my team as part of the ADF Parliamentary Program. Since its introduction in 2003, the parliamentary program with the Australian Defence Force has given ADF members the opportunity to step outside their usual working environment and gain a unique insight into how decisions are debated and made in this place. It also works the other way, and for many of us as parliamentarians I know quite a few senators in the chamber this evening have participated in and had the opportunity to meet people in the ADF and hear directly about their experiences.

Flight Lieutenant Evans joined the Royal Australian Air Force back in 2019, I'm reliably informed, as an aspiring armament engineer officer. His work involves integrating and assessing weapons and countermeasure systems across a range of ADF aircraft and platforms. It's an area that we need a lot more men and women in our ADF to work in. It's a very technical role but a very important one that ultimately comes down to making sure our personnel have the systems and the technology that keep our aircraft safe, capable and ready to operate. It is great to have him spend the week in my office. I thank him for his contributions, and I'm sure he's finding his time here in the parliament—and in the chamber this evening—worthwhile. Welcome.

I also take this opportunity to recognise another important contribution to Australia's national security. Twenty-five years ago, the Australian Strategic Policy Institute began with a deceptively simple idea—that Australia's strategic policy would be better if the thinking behind it was contested, not comfortable. ASPI's establishment back in 2001 was a genuinely bipartisan undertaking. We saw, a few weeks ago, former prime minister John Howard and former opposition leader Kim Beazley reflect on that founding spirit, writing that ASPI has consistently exerted a positive influence on Australia's security policy and that spirit above politics and in the national interest has shaped ASPI into what it is today—and it is continuing to grow with much respect.

Over more than two decades, ASPI's researchers have challenged thinking on border security, on terrorism, on critical minerals and on defence preparedness, and put climate and food security on the national agenda before it was fashionable to do so. That same spirit led to the establishment of ASPI's Women in Defence and Security Network back in 2014, opening doors and building pathways for women in defence, national security and foreign policy.

I pay tribute to and acknowledge the outgoing executive director, Justin Bassi, who last week advised that he will be leaving the organisation. Under Justin's leadership, ASPI has built resilience through a period of profound international disruption, from research on artificial intelligence and the Indo-Pacific to convening the Sydney Dialogue on critical technologies. I thank him for his service and, on a personal note, wish him very well for his future with his family. He is someone that I consider a friend and a mentor on these policies on national security and defence.

The strategic environment of 2026 bears little resemblance to that of 2001, and that only makes ASPI's role more important and more necessary. As ASPI marks 25 years, let the next 25 be defined by the same founding spirit and courage to challenge conventional thinking. I congratulate ASPI on its contribution to Australia's national security debate and the strategic debate more broadly.

speaker: Sarah Hanson-Young
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: These guardrails are of course important, but big AI are railroading communities now and getting their approvals for their centres now. Will your government either put in place a moratorium or make your laws retrospective? Otherwise, how can the Australian people trust you?

speaker: Allegra Spender
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS
text:
In the last week, we've seen leaders in the world's pioneer AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI paint an alarming picture of the speed at which technology is developing, potentially beyond human controls. These CEOs spoke about their concerns and also their own responsibilities but they are calling on governments around the world to step up into this space, and I believe that this is urgent. I want to put on the record very strongly that I think that Australia needs to embrace AI. I recognise the benefits. I believe that Australian businesses need to seize the opportunities for productivity, and, if we don't, we will be left behind. I see the role for data centres in our country, both from a sovereign capability piece but also because of the potential benefits to the energy grid and the clean energy transition.

But we also need to be honest about the risks and we need to be addressing those actively. I know that my community is concerned. I launched a survey earlier this week about AI and already have had hundreds of responses. An overwhelming number, 71 per cent, said they were very concerned about AI in general and listed catastrophic risks such as AI takeover, AI-enabled terrorism or extreme threats as their No. 1 concern, and other concerns included misinformation, disinformation and threats to democracy, environmental and climate impacts, job losses and economic disruption. The vast majority of respondents, 84 per cent, said that the government was not doing nearly enough to appropriately deal with the risks of AI. To be honest, I do agree with this. The government has been very slow to act. It took them until the end of last year to bring in an AI strategy, despite being in government for an entire term without one. Other governments have moved faster than them and this was slow. The government seems to be paying more attention now, and I welcome that, but it still has a long way to go.

I want to talk about four things I think the government needs to step up on. Firstly, it needs to step up on AI safety. My understanding is that currently the AI Safety Institute, which the government established, has a budget of around $30 million over four years. People are putting the risk that AI destroys humanity at around 10 per cent. It doesn't seem like we are being serious about the potential impact of AI when we're managing the risks with so little money.

Secondly, Australia needs to work with other middle powers on this. USA and China are leading the way, but we must work with other middle powers in terms of making sure that we have a role and a step and a control in this space. Finally, we need to actively capture the benefits much more strongly. That means not only helping Australian businesses but also setting ourselves challenges, like how AI can solve national problems and national concerns, some national missions that AI can deliver to really improve our society as well.

speaker: Lord Alton of Liverpool
heading: AI: Human Extinction - Question
text: My Lords, in light of the existential threats referred to by the noble Baroness, Lady Teather, and having chaired the inquiry launched by the Joint Committee on Human Rights into AI and human rights, with 10 oral sessions, including important evidence from Minister Kanishka Narayan, may I ask the Minister whether she will urgently read this 94-page report, published yesterday and now available in the Printed Paper Office? Having particular regard to its 59 recommendations and conclusions on the inadequacy of existing law and regulations, will she ensure a swift response and that we will have the opportunity to debate this report fully in your Lordships’ House?

speaker: Josh Burns
heading: COMMITTEES
subheading: Public Accounts and Audit Joint Committee; Report
text:
On behalf of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit, I present the following reports: Report 516: Inquiry into Commonwealth financial statements 2023-24 and 2024-25 and Report 517: Annual report 2025-26.

Report made a parliamentary paper in accordance with standing order 39(e).

by leave—First of all, I present the report of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit No. 516: Inquiry into Commonwealth financial statements 2023-24 and 2024-25.

The annual auditing of financial accounting and reporting by Commonwealth entities by the Australian National Audit Office provides assurance to the parliament on the financial position of the Australian government and the expenditure of taxpayer money.

This report considers the findings of both the 2023-24 and 2024-25 financial statements audits, with a particular focus on three areas of interest to the committee: compliance with legislation, including section 83 of the Australian Constitution; the information technology environment; and the governance of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.

Legislative non-compliance has increased across the two audit periods. While the committee welcomes evidence that entities have accepted the seriousness of issues identified by the ANAO, and are taking active steps toward remediation, the committee remains concerned by the number of breaches that persist across multiple audit cycles.

The IT control environment continues to account for the largest proportion of audit findings. It is clear to the committee that IT governance and controls continue to be a persistent challenge for entities.

The committee was encouraged by the approaches undertaken by the Department of Defence and NBN Co, both of which have successfully resolved findings relating to unauthorised post-separation access of IT networks. In these cases, resolution was achieved by addressing the issue as a whole-of-business issue rather than one confined to IT alone. The committee considers this approach instructive for the broader public sector and encourages other entities to apply similar methods.

The committee also considered the continued growth in the use of AI and other emerging technologies across the public sector. While the committee did not investigate the use of AI across the public sector in depth, it will continue to monitor whether governance frameworks are keeping pace with the rate of adoption and the range of emerging use cases.

One recommendation made by the committee was that the ANAO tables at least annually a report that examines public sector entities use and preparedness for emerging digital technologies.

I want to acknowledge and thank Senator Matt O'Sullivan for his service as deputy chair until March 2026 and thank the current deputy chair, the Hon. Scott Buchholz MP, for his help, commitment and support.

I thank all committee members for their contributions to this inquiry, and I commend that report to the House.

I am also pleased to present Report 517: Annual report 2025-26I've already given it to the clerks.

Under the Public Accounts and Audit Committee Act 1951, the committee is required to report annually to the parliament on the work it has undertaken.

The committee's work includes reviewing Australian National Audit Office reports and conducting inquiries where it identifies issues needing further examination. The committee determines the audit priorities of the parliament and makes recommendations to the government on the budget estimates of the Australian National Audit Office and the Parliamentary Budget Office. The committee can request a post-election review of the PBO's operations and did so following the 2025 election.

In 2025-26, the committee held 27 meetings, including seven public hearings. The committee commenced eight inquiries, tabled three reports, undertook a range of non-inquiry activities in line with legislative responsibilities and met with delegations from Kiribati and Cambodia, both highly successful. We completed inquiries in 2025-26, including into the effectiveness of Australia's National Anti-Doping Scheme and the procurement processes for supporting services for victims of child sexual abuse.

Again, I thank the deputy chair and all of the committee members, and I also want to pay a special tribute to the secretariat, who are outstanding public servants and serve the committee with distinction.

I commend the report to the House.

I ask leave of the House to present executive minutes on reports of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit, if that's possible.

Leave granted.

I present the executive minutes on reports 463, 472, 477, 479, 485, 486, 488, 491, 492, 498, 502, 504, 509, 511, 512, 514 and 515 of the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit.

speaker: Basem Abdo
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
text:
I thank the member for Curtin for bringing this matter of public importance here today. AI is essential policy conversation across the world that demands our full attention. When it comes to AI, we as a government are driven by progress and principles. We agree that this emerging technology represents a generational opportunity for Australia if properly harnessed. It presents immense opportunities just as it carries significant risks, and our focus on progress and principles means that our approach as a government is to engage with both simultaneously with seriousness and urgency. It is relevant to our economy, workforce, national security and online safety as well as research, science, innovation and the productivity of our economy.

When it comes to action, this government is taking world-leading action guided by a clear set of principles. The Albanese government's National AI Plan sets out three key pillars which are focused on capturing the opportunity before us, sharing in its benefits and keeping Australians safe. As announced by the Prime Minister, the government will introduce AI laws in Australia's interests—a nationally consistent regulatory framework that will work with the states and territories to set minimum requirements for large data centres. This world-leading framework will ensure Australia can capture the opportunity, share the benefits and keep Australians safe.

Over the past nine months alone, the government has released the National AI Plan; released national expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure; established the AI Safety Institute; announced that Australia will legislate AI safety and a world-leading artificial intelligence framework to ensure that the development of AI in Australia is aligned with our interests; established the Office of AI in the Prime Minister's department to deliver the development of the standards; and established a 'buy Australian' initiative for Australian-made AI. The Prime Minister will be at the UN General Assembly next week, where a key focus of his will be technology regulation. The Deputy Prime Minister and Assistant Minister Charlton also recently travelled to the United States to engage on Australia's national AI standards and issues to do with AI safety. It's an all-hands-on-deck effort, engaging every part of the government.

I have previously spoken about a proposed large-scale data centre in Campbellfield, on the site of the old Ford plant, in my electorate. I have stressed the need for communities like mine to understand what impact this development may have on our local area, including the potential impact on local energy and water resources and ongoing noise, as well as whether this is the best use of what was a key manufacturing hub for our community. I was devastated when the Liberals drove Ford and local jobs on that site out of our area, and that site means a lot to me and to our community. We all remember the workers who were there, who made things in Australia and who, in doing so, helped make Australia. When it comes to AI, it should be done the Australian way—without undercutting conditions or dividing communities or damaging our environment. Major industrial developments need to contribute to local jobs and local opportunities and must take into account our local environment and the future of our region.

As AI demand and reliance on cloud computing grow, data centre investment in our area must happen in ways that deliver positive outcomes for our community. While planning decisions and approvals are not a matter for federal government, I have made it clear that the Albanese Labor government has set out clear expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure to ensure that investments provide tangible benefits, both locally and across Australia. Operators must prioritise Australia's national interests not only by strengthening our security and resilience but also by delivering benefits for our local communities. Any proposal will be required to bring additional renewable energy to power their site, and we're acting to make sure they don't put upward pressure on energy prices with our world-leading rules.

They will also be expected to manage water responsibly, create well paid local jobs and skills, and back startups and research innovation and supply chains. Data centre developments must meet these expectations. Our community deserves clear answers, genuine consultation and transparent planning processes aligned with the federal government's clear expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure. I will continue to advocate strongly for our area and for the long-term liveability, sustainability and wellbeing of our growing community, just as the Albanese government is fully engaged on the opportunities and risks presented by AI.

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text:
I thank the member for Barton for her question. Indeed, AI offers extraordinary opportunities for Australia, for our growth, for investment, for productivity and for businesses such as those I'll speak with tonight at the Australian Industry Group about using AI to benefit their productivity and therefore to be able to grow. Our government knows that, and that's why we're legislating Australian standards for AI. That's why we're also consulting across the board, engaging seriously with other nations as well as with AI companies themselves, so we can make sure that AI stands for Australia's interests, harnessing its power as a tool to help us build a stronger economy.

We know that we need humanity to shape AI rather than the other way around. That is why we've established the AI committee that has been stood-up in a bipartisan fashion and has already begun its work under the leadership of the member for Maribyrnong and Senator Duniam in the other place. The hack by a frontier AI agent into government websites brought home to Australians that some of the risks which are there are very real indeed. We took strong action on that and made our nation's view clear that the breach was completely unacceptable.

It is clear for everyone to see that the AI genie is well and truly out of the bottle. We can't pretend that it doesn't exist and isn't already having an impact on the way that we work, the way that we engage and, indeed, the way that politics is conducted as well. That is why what really matters is how we respond to it and how we intervene and shape it. That is also why we are engaging with domestic and global companies and with other nations as well. We did that at the United Nations General Assembly last month. We did that as well in the meetings that we have continued to hold with major companies. We're going to make sure that Australia can gain from the benefits that can come from AI whilst mitigating the risks. That is the way forward, that is what is in Australia's national interest, and that is what we will continue to do. I encourage every member of this House to engage with this process because this will be one of the dominant issues over the next decade and beyond.

speaker: David Pocock
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE
text: I've got another question for the Minister for Industry and Innovation, Senator Ayres. Minister, OpenAI told the Joint Select Committee on AI that they would be providing Australia with red-level access to their Daybreak cyber program. When will Australia get this access, and how much will it cost us?

speaker: Perran Moon
subheading: Royal Mail: Performance — [Emma Lewell in the Chair]
text:
Meur ras, Ms Lewell. It is an honour to serve under your chairship. I thank the hon. Member for Lagan Valley (Sorcha Eastwood) for securing this debate and for her excellent speech.

The performance of Royal Mail in Camborne, Redruth and Hayle, in the south-west of Cornwall, has been simply woeful. Constituents regularly tell me that they have gone weeks without post and, like other hon. Members’ constituents, have received a large backlog all at once.

Sharon from Hayle had waited a year for an operation when she received a call from the hospital asking whether she intended to attend. The appointment letter, together with the swabs required pre surgery, had never arrived. Thankfully, the arrangements were later confirmed by phone and email, but the letter itself was delivered three days after the operation had taken place. Another constituent was sent a letter for a hospital appointment 19 days after it was scheduled. Such delays risk causing vulnerable people to miss essential treatment, and place a burden on our overstretched NHS.

In Cornwall, our remote coastal geography and patchy digital connectivity—to say the least—mean that many of us still rely heavily on the universal postal service, but I worry that the situation will only get worse. In recent weeks, several Royal Mail workers have contacted me with concerns about the new delivery model 26. They report unmanageable workloads, experienced workers leaving, morale at rock bottom and substantial volumes of mail sitting undelivered. Three workers completing four rounds does not sound a credible way to improve reliability and restore public trust in Royal Mail. I echo the points made: the issue is not one of posties; it is one of management. Nor should Royal Mail continue to respond, if at all, to our constituents with template responses or hide behind impossible-to-navigate AI chatbots, while the reality on the ground slips further behind.

I therefore ask the Minister what discussions the Government have had with Royal Mail about DM26, and what action will be taken to ensure my constituents receive a postal service worthy of the word “royal”. If Royal Mail is going to treat this House and elected Members with such arrogance, the Government must take direct, firm and urgent action.

speaker: Lord Ponsonby of Shulbrede
heading: Procedural Flexibility: Scrutiny of AI and Emerging Technology - Question
text: My Lords, our procedures allow flexibility, including topical Oral Questions, Private Notice Questions and Questions for Written Answer. The Government also offer regular statements, and Urgent Questions asked in the House of Commons are often repeated in your Lordships’ House. The noble Lord himself has used a number of these avenues to raise matters related to AI. The Procedure and Privileges Committee has not discussed scrutiny of AI and emerging technology. However, it is open to considering any proposals.

speaker: Lord Holmes of Richmond
heading: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill - Report
text:
My Lords, I apologise for not getting to my feet before our Front Bench. I was clearly so moved by the eloquence and erudition of the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, that it slowed my motor function, and by the speed of my noble friend Lord Camrose, who clearly has his Asics on today. I very much support Amendment 61. There is so much talk about AI sovereignty, data sovereignty and digital sovereignty with it potentially meaning different things to each speaker of the sovereignty spiel. We need greater clarity across this. In the Bill before us, having this comprehensive clause covering what is required when it comes to digital sovereignty for the United Kingdom makes complete sense.

Moving to the Computer Misuse Act, the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, my noble friend Lord Arbuthnot, I and others have pushed various Governments over at least a decade on this issue. Our cyber professionals, those who do so much to keep us safe, often and understandably in silence and in the shadows, deserve our support. It cannot be that they are still on the wrong side of a statute that is racing towards its 40th birthday. We should update the Computer Misuse Act. The noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, has offered a pragmatic solution in his proposed new clause, with a 12-month period to bring this to fruition. Our cyber professionals do so much; they deserve our support. This proportionate amendment should be accepted by the Government and put in the Bill.

speaker: Ali France
heading: BILLS
subheading: Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
Continuing on from earlier, these laws are about protecting people from harm. They're about setting basic standards and giving social media users more choice over what they see. It will require big tech to provide a safe online environment, in particular for our kids. Our country needs this; our kids need this.

This month, the AFP has told us about and spoken of online child exploitation and victimisation, like on nudify apps. They've also spoken about online abuse and accounts; the manosphere; images and videos that glorify violence, porn and misogyny; and content that encourages eating disorders. Suicide is having a devastating impact, and all of this content is having a devastating impact on our kids. It has real-world consequences.

I spoke earlier about the number of comments that I receive on my social media accounts. If you had a side look at my socials for a minute, you'd see that, over the last 18 months, I've had tens of thousands of comments threatening my personal safety, calling me 'peg leg', calling me 'NDIS scum' and telling me that they hope my other son dies. Last week, one person wrote:

know where your family lives, run or burn

which was reported to the AFP. In the week before, Adrian said:

you are a delusional—

bleep—

retard that needs a hot poker shove up your—

bleep. John said:

jump off a building already—

bleep bleep. Jamie said:

I prefer assassinations.

Leroy said:

Someone shoot this dopey—

bleep. And, on the day after Helen's attack, Josh said:

are you gonna get the AFP to knock on my door for 'intimidating you'

We know that words and other content online and in the media fuel violence, threats and abuse in real life, not just for MPs but for teachers, health workers and retail workers. The Minister for Social Services, Tanya Plibersek, said yesterday that the explosion in social media tracks the explosion of sexual violence and strangulation. It's frightening. Kids, vulnerable people and people with mental health issues read those comments. They see and they feel the hate. They follow and are fed destructive content. There are millions of social media accounts that promote and normalise violence, misogyny, extremism and dangerous behaviours—porn.

We must demand better from big tech and the online environment. That is at the core of this legislation. If you run an online service in this country, you have a duty to keep the people using it safe. If you build it and put it online, you are responsible for the risks to users. And it's not just about social media; the games, the apps and the AI chatbots are all covered by this bill, as are nudify apps, which we heard today over 200,000 people have downloaded in Australia. That's scary.

We know what algorithms feed our young people: content that promotes eating disorders; content that glorifies dangerous behaviour, violence and suicide; and content promoting misogyny and the abuse of women. This content is seeping out of the screen and into our schools, our homes and our relationships. These are accounts that are, overwhelmingly, set up to menace and harass. Teachers are telling us about it. Young female teachers are now copping abuse in the classroom. They are telling us about attitudes that walk through the school gate straight off a phone or an iPad. It is content that radicalises, pushing young people towards extremism and violence.

This bill creates a single, overarching obligation—a digital duty of care. It requires the providers of online services to take reasonable, practicable steps to keep the people who use them safe. A duty of care is not a new idea; it is one of the oldest ideas in our legal system. We already ask an employer to take reasonable steps to keep their workers safe. We ask the builder to make safe homes and the manufacturer to make safe products. All this bill does is apply the same well-settled principle to online services that are now as much a part of our daily life as any workplace or public square The standard is not perfection. The standard is what is reasonably practicable—reasonable steps matched to the risk. That is a deliberate choice, because for too long the approach to online safety in this country has been to just politely ask the platforms, 'Do better,' with a set of basic online safety expectations and industry codes. They were a start. But, as we all know, that approach has been a big fat fail.

This bill replaces that with one clear, enforceable duty, set by this parliament, that every provider must meet. For young people, this bill goes further still. Providers must take particular care to protect Australians under 18 from the harmful material they promote. Where a platform breaches that duty of care it will face penalties of up to $109 million, enforced by the independent eSafety Commissioner. The bill also gives the eSafety Commissioner strong tools to act on the harms that are hurting Australians right now. It sets minimum standards for how complaints and disputes are handled so that, when an Australian reports something, they get a proper process and a real response, not a bot and a dead end.

This builds on the work the Albanese Labor government has already done to make Australians safer online with the social media minimum age and our crackdown on nudify apps and undetectable tracking tools that are used to stalk and control women. Then there is the part of the bill that hands Aussies back some direct control. We call it My Feed, My Way. Under the bill, social media services will have to notify their users—new users and existing users alike—and offer them a real choice over what drives their main feed, an opportunity to shut out the garbage, to switch it off. You can absolutely keep the algorithm and swallow that garbage if you want to, but if you don't want to you can choose not to: your feed, your choice. This bill gives you the power to make it social again, to make it about your friends, your family, your favourite charities and the businesses you want to follow.

Now, you would think that a law to protect Aussies from this would be a no-brainer, but we know that those opposite and One Nation will tell you this bill is censorship. They'll call it Big Brother. They will say that the government is coming for your freedom—which is just rubbish. Adults can still access what they want. The real freedom is in the ability to switch off the algorithm. We would not accept the harms caused online in other environments and other contexts. We demand that a car is safe before it is sold. We demand that a medication is tried and tested before it is put to the market. We demand that a toy is safe before a child can play with it. We should demand nothing less of the platforms Australians use every single day.

At the centre of this bill is one simple principle: that the best interests of Aussies should come first. On this side of the House we are choosing the wellbeing of the people who use these platforms over the profits of the companies that run them. Anyone who votes against this bill is choosing something else. They are choosing profit. They are choosing outrage. They are choosing harm. I know which side I'm on, and I commend this bill to the House.

speaker: Tania Lawrence
heading: BILLS
subheading: Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text:
I rise to support the Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026. The bill should be understood as part of something much larger. It is yet another positive step in the transformation of Australia's defence posture that has been underway since the Albanese Labor government took office.

We are spending more on defence, but the challenge before Australia is not simply to spend more on defence. It is to identify the capabilities our nation needs, acquire them faster, build and sustain more of them here at home, reduce sovereign risk, firm up supply chains, work effectively with our allies and trusted partners, and protect those capabilities, the people behind them and, importantly, the places from which they operate. That takes investment, and this government is providing it at a level unprecedented in living memory. But it also takes strategy, industry, skills, partnerships, accountability and, saliently, laws that are fit for the strategic environment in which the Australian Defence Force now operates.

The bill establishes a new defence capability framework to support capability development, testing, evaluation and preparedness, alongside a defence security zone framework to better protect defence personnel, the facilities, the information, the activities and the capabilities. Importantly, the bill also provides for independent oversight by the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force.

I've spoken in this House before about Australia facing the most challenging strategic circumstances since the Second World War. In fact, there are more conflicts right now than there ever have been since the Second World War. This is not a slogan. It is the starting point for serious defence policy—policy based on our own needs and interests and the development of a sovereign capability.

Since 2022, the Albanese government has been systematically answering some fundamental questions: What kind of Defence Force does Australia need? What capabilities must it possess? How rapidly must we acquire them? What must Australia do to build and sustain ourselves? And how do we make our Defence Force, our economy, our infrastructure and our communities more resilient? There is a clear chronology to what then followed.

In 2022, one of the first actions of the Albanese Labor government was to commission the Defence Strategic Review, led independently by former defence minister and former foreign minister Professor Stephen Smith and former Chief of the Defence Force, Sir Angus Houston. I know both of these men, and I know the seriousness and the expertise they bring to their work. That review was commissioned within the government's first 100 days. We did not begin with an arbitrary spending figure. We began by examining Australia's strategic circumstances, determining the force structure needed to respond to them, and then identifying the capabilities required to make that force credible.

The Defence Strategic Review was released in April 2023. It identified six priorities for immediate action: nuclear powered submarines, through AUKUS; longer range strike and Australian munitions manufacturing; strengthening our northern bases; growing and retaining the defence workforce; translating disruptive technologies into military capability more rapidly; and deepening Australia's diplomatic and defence relationships across the Indo-Pacific. As I've said previously in this House, thanks indeed to the extraordinary leadership of ministers Marles, Conroy, Keogh, Kahlil and Thistlethwaite, a great deal has followed on from that strategic review process.

In March 2023, Australia, the United States and the United Kingdom announced the AUKUS optimal pathway. That pathway provides for increasing submarine visits; the Submarine Rotational Force-West, from as early as next year; Australia's acquisition of Virginia class submarines, from the early 2030s; and, ultimately, the construction of SSN-AUKUS. For Western Australia, this is very real. HMAS Stirling will sit at the centre of the Submarine Rotational Force-West, with a planned rotational presence from as early as next year of one UK and up to four US conventionally armed and nuclear powered submarines. That means infrastructure, engineers, apprentices, nuclear stewardship, security, maintenance, sustainment and Australian supply chains. It means the development of sovereign Australian capability.

In April 2024, the government delivered Australia's first national defence strategy, establishing a strategy of denial as the cornerstone of defence planning and directing the ADF towards becoming an integrated, focused force. Modern deterrence requires integration across maritime, land, air space and cyber domains. It requires intelligence, resilient infrastructure and supply chains, advanced technology and a strong Australian industrial base, and that requires investment. The 2024 National Defence Strategy provided an additional $5.7 billion over four years and $50.3 billion over the decade above the previous Defence funding trajectory. The Australian Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Plan committed $16 billion to $21 billion across the decade, including Australian manufacture of the Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System missiles and maintenance of the Naval Strike and Joint Strike missiles. Buying capability is one thing; being able to replenish it, repair it, modify it and sustain it in a crisis is another.

That same year, Labor also introduced legislation for a dedicated Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence modelled in significant respects to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, on which I serve, and able to deal with the classified information. A statutory Defence committee had been a bipartisan recommendation actually over several parliamentary reports. When we build capability, we also have to build proper parliamentary oversight. The coalition, unfortunately though, played politics and failed to support the bill at that time and delayed the establishment of the committee.

In 2025, much of this planning became increasingly tangible. In January, the government committed another $262 million to develop Australia's AUKUS submarine supply chain, supporting around 125 Australian businesses with the skills, security, accreditation, manufacturing, equipment and qualifications for international submarine supply chains. Then, in September, the Prime Minister announced $12 billion in new funding for the Henderson defence precinct in Western Australia. By then the additional Defence investment over the decade had reached $70 billion.

Henderson will support continuous naval ship building, AUKUS, surface-vessel sustainment and future submarine support, with the government projecting more than 10,000 local jobs. On any visit there, you will see the place and how it's transforming. The energy, the absolute dedication and focus across all tiers of government—local, state and federal—is actually an extraordinary example of how we can work fast and collaboratively where it's needed on such a priority project.

The Prime Minister spoke of investment in both our capability and our relationships. That is an important distinction. Sovereign capability does not mean strategic isolation. Australian capability becomes stronger when Australian industry and workers are connected to the technology, the expertise and the scale of trusted partners. We are also seeing emerging technology move from theory to practice. During Exercise Talisman Sabre in July 2025, AUKUS partners deployed autonomous and remotely operated underwater vehicles and advanced algorithms aboard an Australian P-8 maritime patrol aircraft. Later that year, more than 200 defence personnel, scientists and industry participants tested around 30 next-generation capabilities through Maritime Big Play.

In December, the government announced major reform of capability acquisition and sustainment, including the creation of a dedicated Defence Delivery Agency and Australia's first National Armaments Director. Labor also reinforced the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence legislation in October 2025, and it finally passed both houses on 4 March this year. So today Australia has a statutory Parliamentary Joint Committee on Defence with legislative scrutiny and parliamentary oversight, and that matters. The larger Defence becomes, the more sophisticated its capabilities become and the more tax money we obviously invest, so a stronger case is made for rigorous parliamentary oversight. Supporting Defence and scrutinising Defence are not competing objectives. Strong accountability makes Defence stronger.

Then we come to this year. The government has again increased the scale and pace of reform. The 2026 National defence strategy and Integrated Investment Program bring the combined additional investment to $117 billion over the decade to 2035-36. The 2026 strategy places greater emphasis on self-reliance, sovereign industrial resilience, international industrial partnerships, national civil preparedness and resilience. Under the NATO methodology, Defence spending is projected to reach three per cent of GDP by 2033. That is why the acquisition reforms matter.

The Defence Delivery Group commenced on 1 July 2026, with reforms intended to provide clearer accountability, stronger contestability and better cost estimation and assurance as Defence transitions towards the Defence Delivery Agency. The government's Rebuilding defence capability report says that with increased investment comes a clear responsibility to ensure Defence has the structures, the skills and the systems necessary to turn that strategy into real capability for the ADF. That task, of course, is made more urgent by the speed of technological change. Artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, quantum technology, hypersonics, long-range strike, undersea warfare and directed energy systems are developing extraordinarily quickly.

That brings us directly back to the bill. Modern military capability is increasingly developed with Australian companies, scientists, universities, researchers, engineers, startups, major primes and international partners. The new Defence Capability Framework provides a statutory foundation for developing, testing, evaluating and sustaining that capability. But speed must not come at the expense of safeguards, so the framework does not authorise military operations, intelligence collection or law enforcement activity, nor does it create a general exemption from Australian law or remove environmental heritage or native title protections.

The Defence Security Zone Framework addresses the other half of the equation: protecting what we build. Existing Defence security laws were written in years past, and Defence has identified gaps and inconsistencies, including in responding to contemporary threats such as drone incursions. It makes little sense to spend billions developing sophisticated military capabilities while leaving the people, the places and the technology supporting them vulnerable because our laws have not kept pace. The bill addresses that gap.

I just want to return to WA, because for Western Australia sovereign capability is already becoming real. Henderson and HMAS Stirling, as I said, are central to the story, but so are Western Australian businesses. I've spoken previously in this House about Hofmann Engineering in Ashfield and Bayswater, in my electorate of Hasluck, becoming the first qualified Australian company to receive a request for a quote to supply parts into the United States submarine supply chain. The Hofmann story demonstrates what sovereign capability can mean. A business that began as a backyard operation developed into an internationally connected Australian engineering company—Australian engineering, Australian workers and Australian skills connected into one of the most sophisticated defence industrial networks in the world. That is what AUKUS can look like in an Australian suburb, and that is why defence industry policy is a national security policy. Our security depends not just on what Australia can buy but on what we can build, what we can repair and what we can sustain and replenish.

Amid all of these strategies, investment programs, submarines, missiles and technologies, we should never lose sight of one thing: Defence is ultimately about people. Before coming to this place, I served in the signals reserves, and that experience gave me an enduring appreciation of the responsibilities that come with service and of the people who put on our nation's uniform. Since coming to parliament, I have continued to maintain that connection, including through Exercise Pitch Black, the ADF exchange programs and hosting officers from the ADF through the ADF parliamentary internship program. I'm also engaged through the ANU national security program, and I encourage every MP and senator in this place to participate in the same.

So this bill matters. Capability matters because we may ask our Australian service men and women to use it. I will conclude by saying that we are working now to develop that capability faster and to protect the capability better. I commend the bill to the House.

speaker: Peter Kyle
heading: Income Tax (Charge)
text:
The right hon. Gentleman’s intervention was longer than my speech has been so far. When I find that I agree with every word that somebody is saying, I usually sit down and listen to a bit more of it rather than trying to challenge it. Perhaps the rest of my speech will answer the questions that he raises.

In that decade, because of the predictability and certainty of growth, I think that growth policy was seen like any other policy. In other words, if there was a shelf with all the different policies of Government on it, growth would be one set of policies on that shelf. I know that there are a lot of analogies going around these days, and Liz Truss has blown a hole in analogy use as well as in our economy, but it is my belief that we now need to have the mindset that growth is the shelf itself. We cannot have successful social policies delivered in the way that all of us in this Chamber would like unless we have a solid, predictably-growing economy into the long term that provides security and prosperity and from which we can share investment fairly around the country.

We must on both sides of the House be as animated about economic growth as we are about creating prosperity, spending it and challenging the social ills in our society. We must care as much about economic growth as we do about rough sleeping, social care and international development—I say that as someone who spent my early life in international development. Tackling those issues depends on economic growth itself.

Public services are incredibly important. They are enablers of growth. We cannot have growth if people are arriving late to work, are too sick to work or are stuck on a Tory waiting list for treatment. We need to have the right skills in the right places. All of those things are absolutely essential, but we should not kid ourselves that such growth is not built on by private enterprise.

Thanks to the Prime Minister deciding that I could have some time over the summer, I was able to write an essay—now that Tony Blair has brought them back into fashion. I know that many Members will have already read it, making some of my words today obsolete, but let me refresh their minds about what I focused on. I confined the essay to my experience in Government and how we can configure Government more assiduously and dependably to unlock the economic growth that our country needs so much—focusing on what Government themselves can deliver. That experience comes from leading two Departments as Secretary of State. I saw in both those Departments that civil servants can deliver boldly when they have the authority to and when incentives align.

I will use one example—the automotive sector—to illustrate to Members the challenges that the Government face to unlock growth. Delivering support for the automotive sector means aligning energy, trade, regulation and all these different areas of policy. All are held by more than one Government Department, and each of those Departments has its own priorities. As Secretary of State in the Department for Business and Trade, at times I was prioritising the automotive sector and recognising how important it can be for growth. Let us bear in mind, when Jaguar Land Rover suffered its cyber-attack, 0.2% was taken off our GDP. When it was up and running six weeks later, 0.2% was returned to our GDP. The importance of industry is still fundamental. When the Prime Minister and the Chancellor talk about reindustrialisation, hon. Members should not underestimate its ability to deliver growth for our overall economy.

We have another asset when it comes to the automotive sector in our country. When we talk about frontier technology—I am looking for the Minister for Artificial Intelligence, who was in his place a moment ago—we think about the AI labs, most of which are in California, with some in China, but we have a frontier industry here in the UK in the automotive sector, and it is Formula 1, because 11 of the 12 teams do all their research and development and all the deployment of their vehicles right here in the UK. No other country in the world has that asset, and that filters skills through our automotive sector. The ability to grow that sector is huge, but that needs Government to work in an aligned way.

I discovered how different Departments with different priorities have oversight over things like automotive, and how sometimes they can slow down those priority areas. We need the structures and incentives in Government to be much better aligned, because we cannot have all these important sectors depending on Ministers’ ability to WhatsApp each other to sort out problems. We should have a system of Government that is already on the side of making pro-growth choices.

I want to say a few brief words about defence, which has already been raised in the debate. I am grateful to the Chancellor for the statements he has made on this. We focus on the percentage of GDP allocated to defence, but the debate cannot just be about how big a share of our economy we spend on defence; it must also be about how big an economy we have. If we were to achieve five years of 3% annual growth, 3% of our national income on defence would deliver almost the same amount of money as moving to 3.5% in an economy of today’s size.

speaker: Scott Arthur
subheading: Social Media: Ban for Under-16s — [Sir Roger Gale in the Chair]
text:
Like so many problems in the world, the solution can be found in Scotland. Young people in Scotland can use a Young Scot card to verify that they are 16, but I understand my hon. Friend’s point.

It is critical that, alongside robust age-assurance measures, online platforms be required to be as safe as possible for all users, both young people and adults. A ban cannot be used as an excuse by companies not to comply with their responsibilities, and important questions remain about the scope of the ban and the regulation of high-risk features. In July, I welcomed the Government’s further commitment to require infinite scrolling features to be switched off by default. However, there is more work to be done on location-sharing features for under-16s, as well as further regulation of AI chatbots.

I accept and understand the point that for some people, such as those who are struggling with mental health problems, health problems or perhaps their sexuality, going to social media may be a source of really good information. However, I am also concerned that young people who go to social media for advice on those really sensitive issues might end up interacting with people whose motivations are not good, and I think we have to be very mindful of that.

speaker: Gareth Davies
heading: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
text:
It is a great pleasure to close this debate on behalf of the official Opposition, and to follow on from my very good friend, the shadow Economic Secretary—my hon. Friend the Member for Wyre Forest (Mark Garnier)—who has done excellent work both in this Chamber and behind the scenes to engage extensively with the industry. Indeed, I am sure there is not a lunch table in the City of London that has not been graced by my hon. Friend—all, of course, in the service of his great country.

I draw the House’s attention to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, particularly my long career in asset management, my active involvement in the industry going back many years, and my current chairmanship of the APPG for blockchain, which is relevant to this Bill.

It has been a privilege to be joined by many Members from across the House who clearly have extensive industry experience. I firmly believe, as I have for a long time, that we need more people in Parliament who have worked specifically in this sector, and who understand its importance and its power to help and influence our economy and our communities.

I thank all Members from across the House for their contributions to the debate, but I will name a few in particular. The Chairman of the Treasury Committee, the hon. Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier) who is not currently in her place, provided a typically detailed and very thoughtful contribution. She expressed concerns about whether the pendulum is swinging away from consumer protection, as well as outlining her concerns about the reforms to the FOS. I do not agree necessarily with everything she said, but the House is better for the scrutiny that she and her Committee provide.

Let me pay tribute to our country’s longest-serving Economic Secretary, my right hon. Friend the Member for Salisbury (John Glen), who moved with grace from museums to MiFID back in the day. He spoke about his mixed views of the FOS. He acknowledged that it is—in his words—an unreliable path to resolution, and helpfully warned us that we need to consider the challenges posed by AI to the financial services sector.

I congratulate the hon. Member for Peterborough (Andrew Pakes) on his appointment as the Government’s co-operatives and mutuals champion. I have to say it is an appointment that passed me by, but I very much welcome it. One person who has always been a champion of co-operatives and mutuals is, of course, the hon. Member for Harrow West (Gareth Thomas), who spoke of the high cost and burden of credit, especially for those in poverty.

We on the Conservative side of the House want sensible deregulation. We want less bureaucracy in our system. We want lower burdens and more growth. Where the Bill does that, we will welcome it and we will help make it happen. The Chancellor was right in his opening remarks when he said that it is important to recognise the cross-party work that has gone on already with the Bill. He rightly echoed the views of those us on the Conservative Benches when it was said in the other place that the Bill moves us all in the right direction. Having said that—I am loath to depart from the happy and collegiate atmosphere of the debate so far—I am reminded of what Disraeli once said:

“No Government can be long secure without a formidable Opposition.”

So, if Members will forgive me, I have a job to do tonight. In certain areas, as my hon. Friend the Member for Wyre Forest set out, we believe the Bill does not go far enough. I would like to highlight two areas in particular.

First, on digital assets, the United States has legislated for stablecoin. South Korea and even the European Union have their own regimes. Our competitors globally are moving ahead. That matters because stablecoins could revolutionise the way we pay for goods and services. Blockchain technologies could transform the way we interact with companies and the state. The Bill was our chance to set out a more advanced vision and policy agenda in those areas, but the Government chose not to.

Secondly, ringfencing forces our largest banks to separate retail banking from the rest of their business. That was right after the financial crisis, but the world has now moved on and our resolution regime has moved on with it, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Salisbury pointed out. If we look at our competitors from New York, Amsterdam, Frankfurt and Paris, not one imposes ringfencing like ours—not one. We believe that we should not either. The Bill gives a little and takes a little, but there is a simpler option. If true deregulation is the aim, we believe the Government should adopt the Conservatives’ plan to scrap ringfencing altogether.

No matter how well intentioned the measures in the Bill are—and I believe they are very well intended— I am afraid that I must point out that they are being brought in alongside a barrage of anti-growth taxation and regulatory burdens imposed on our financial services sector and British business more widely. This afternoon, the Chancellor praised Britain’s financial services sector, and I welcome his words; 13 days ago, he spoke similar words but then doubled the bank surcharge—a £1.5 billion hit to the very companies and people he says he supports.

It is all about choice. The Chancellor could have chosen to cut welfare, which is spiralling above £400 billion, but he chose the easier route for a Labour Chancellor, as my right hon. Friend the Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) said, and decided to tax one of our country’s most-important sectors. Be in no doubt that this will have an impact, and specifically, I fear it will lead to more bank branch closures on our high streets, which none of us in this House wants.

I have no doubt that the Economic Secretary will shortly reference banking hubs in her wind-up, speaking with pride about how the Government are rolling out more. She is right to welcome them—I welcome them too—but she should also be clear about who pays for them. Banking hubs are funded by the banks—every one of them. Cash Access UK is funded by the banks. The mobile libraries and the pop-ups in our communities are funded by the banks. We cannot celebrate banking hubs on a Tuesday and then the next day tax the companies that pay for them. I am in favour of banking hubs, but I would much rather the branches not be closed in the first place.

To her credit, the Economic Secretary understands the sector. She is respected in the City and she understands the importance of banks to our high streets, which makes it all the more disappointing for the sector that she did not act to prevent the latest tax raid. The high street bank tax is just one example, but we also have the hike to national insurance and higher taxes on carried interest. That all results in more jobs put at risk, more high street banks closing and investment and innovation heading elsewhere rather than contributing to growth here in Britain.

For the most part, the Conservatives of course welcome the Bill, and we have been clear about that. Sadly, however, it will do little to overcome the barriers and burdens that this Government have inflicted on the financial services sector over the past two years. Warm words cannot undo cold taxes. The world’s capital has a choice about where it goes, and the Government have not acted in our favour. The Chancellor has a choice: he can back the sector or tax it until it becomes uncompetitive, but he simply cannot do both.
